Treatment is primarily supportive. Pharmacologic treatment is only indicated for patients with serotonin syndrome or those with anxiety, agitation, and/or psychosis who fail to respond to environmental modifications and psychotherapy. A
Although hallucinogens all produce similar behavioral and physiological effects, they are chemically diverse and can be divided into three classes based on structural similarities.
Indole alkylamines such as lysergic acid diethylamide (LSD), d-lysergic acid amine (LSA), psilocybin, dimethyltryptamine (DMT) are serotonin receptor agonist/partial agonists.
Psychedelic phenethylamines such as mescaline, 4-methyl-2,5-dimethoxyamphetamine (DOM), and trimethoxyamphetamine (TMA) are serotonin receptor agonists.
Empathogen phenethylamines such as 3,4-methylenedioxy-N-methylamphetamine (MDMA), methylenedioxyamphetamine (MDA) increase serotonin release and inhibit serotonin receptor uptake.
Empathogen-stimulant hybrid phenethylamines such as paramethoxyamphetamine (PMA) increases serotonin release and blocks breakdown via MAO inhibition.
Arylcycloalkylamines such as phencyclidine (PCP) and ketamine are NMDA glutamate receptor antagonists.

Illicit hallucinogens, including the heterogeneous group of new psychoactive substances (NPS), can cause unexpected toxicity due to unknown impurities, intentionally being laced with other substances, or not containing the psychoactive substance they are claimed to be

Cytochrome-2D6 (CYP2D6) is involved with metabolizing several psychoactive substances. CYP2D6 poor metabolizers or those using CYP2D6 inhibitors like MDMA may be more susceptible to acute toxicity and side effects from concurrently used substances and medications also metabolized by CYP2D6.
MDMA can cause malignant hyperthermia with rhabdomyolysis in patients with a genetic mutations on the ryanodine receptor.

Various hallucinogens whose mechanisms are involved with the serotonergic system, such as LSD and MDMA, can cause serotonin syndrome, especially when used with other serotonergic drugs like SSRIs and over-the-counter cough suppressants containing dextromethorphan.

Paramethoxymethamphetamine (PMMA), a known adulterant in "ecstasy" tablets sold illicitly as MDMA, is considerably more toxic than MDMA. PMMA has been associated with serotonin syndrome, multiorgan dysfunction followed by cardiovascular collapse, and a disproportionate number of deaths.

While a limited number of exposures to standard doses of classic psychedelics like psilocybin and LSD generally have few cardiovascular side effects in otherwise health individuals, rare serious adverse cardiovascular events (e.g., myocardial infarction, cardiomyopathy, cardiac arrest, arrythmias, vasoconstriction leading to limb ischemia, and stroke) can occur when used in high doses, mixed with other drugs, and/or in patients with comorbid heart disease.

Risks of hallucinogen toxicity extend beyond acute exposure, especially in those with comorbid neuropsychiatric conditions, and include suicide, mania, persistent psychosis or schizophrenia spectrum disorder, and hallucinogen persisting perception disorder type I & II.
Consider hallucinogen toxicity in patients that present with acute anxiety, aggression, and psychotic behaviors.
Obtain history and objective proof, if possible, of the ingested product, time of ingestion, and quantity ingested.
Interview family, friends, and/or other witnesses regarding events leading up to changes in behavior.
Rule out other possible causes of acute changes in behavior including infection, trauma, or other underlying general medical or psychiatric conditions.

Acute physiologic effects include hypertension, tachycardia, hyperthermia, decreased appetite, nausea/vomiting, dizziness, loss of motor coordination, mydriasis, and in some cases arrythmias and coagulopathy.
Long term effects include "flashbacks" (re-experiencing of drug effects) and recurrent or chronic psychosis, indicating hallucinogen persisting perception disorder type I or II.
See for a summary of characteristics of hallucinogens, as well as signs and symptoms associated with specific hallucinogens.

Laboratory evaluation is recommended for all patients presenting to the emergency department for poisoning who either have severe symptoms or cannot provide a history of recreational use. Results should be used to facilitate supportive care for the patient.

The first tier is serum or plasma tests for acetaminophen, lithium, salicylate, theophylline, valproic acid, carbamazepine, digoxin, phenobarbital, iron, transferrin, ethyl alcohol, methyl alcohol, and ethylene glycol.
The second tier is urine tests for cocaine, opiates, barbiturates, amphetamines, propoxyphene, and phencyclidine (PCP).
Urine tests can be used for detection of hallucinogens but only indicate acute exposure. These tests can not be used to determine chronicity of use.
Urine samples can detect hallucinogens for up to 1 to 4 days following exposure for indole alkylamines and phenethylamines and one to two weeks following exposure for arylcycloalkylamines.
Standard hair tests (hair sample of 1.5 inches) can detect phencyclidine for up 90 days following exposure.

Additional tests can be obtained based on clinical findings, such as fingerstick glucose, pregnancy test, complete blood count, complete metabolic panel, creatine kinase and urine myoglobin if rhabdomyolysis is suspected, brain imaging if head trauma is apparent, lumbar puncture if fever and suspected meningitis, and electrocardiogram if the cardiovascular exam is abnormal.
Patients should be evaluated for serotonin syndrome by history, physical examination, and the Hunter Serotonin Toxicity Criteria.
Address the ABCs (airway, breathing, circulation). Do not give ipecac or activated charcoal without recommendation from a poison center or emergency department.

Acute intoxication is managed by minimizing stimulation. Patient should be placed in a quiet, secluded room with direct supervision. “Talk down therapy” is recommended for patients presenting with anxiety, agitation, or aggression except for patients suspected of PCP toxicity.
There are no antidotes currently available to treat hallucinogen toxicity.
Pharmacologic treatment is only indicated for the management of anxious, agitated, or psychotic patients who fail to respond to psychotherapy.
Treatment of anxiety and agitation: injectable benzodiazepines such as lorazepam 2 to 4 mg intramuscularly every 30 minutes as needed.

Treatment of psychosis and aggression: low doses of injectable antipsychotics such as haloperidol (2 to 5 mg intramuscularly every 30 minutes as needed) or olanzapine (5 to 10 mg intramuscularly; may repeat 2 hours after initial dose and 4 hours after second dose). Electroconvulsive therapy has been rarely used. Avoid using chlorpromazine due to increased risk of hypotension and seizures with PCP toxicity.
Treatment of physiological effects: supportive care for cardiovascular complications, seizures, or gastrointestinal symptoms.
If present, manage serotonin syndrome based on the severity of symptoms.

Full psychiatric, addiction, and neurological evaluation should be performed once the patient has stabilized to assess for residual psychiatric and cognitive symptoms or underlying psychiatric conditions.
People requiring acute, hospital-based care for hallucinogens were at a 2-fold increased risk of death by unintentional drug poisoning.
Individuals with emergency department visits involving hallucinogens had a greater risk of developing a schizophrenia spectrum disorder.
Behavioral and physiological effects of hallucinogens may be present for 1 to 4 hours after ingestion.
Long-term effects of hallucinogens may be seen for months or years following ingestion.
Since treatment is focused on supportive care, the prognosis is the same as the natural history except in rare cases of Hallucinogen Persisting Perception Disorder Type II.
Hallucinogens may have long term effects on cognition and memory.

feature.caption: Summary of Characteristics of Hallucinogens.
feature.feature_body:
Behavioral Effects Physiological Effects Long-Term Effects
Lysergic Acid Diethylamide (LSD), d-Lysergic Acid Amine (LSA), Psilocybin and Dimethyltryptamine (DMT)
Depends on dose and environment Altered sense of time and self Impaired judgment, concentration, and intellectual functioning Hallucinations (predominately visual) Sensation “cross-over” (hearing colors and seeing sounds)
Diaphoresis Reflex bradycardia Respiratory depression GI distress
Flashbacks (up to 1 year following ingestion) Not associated with addiction (self-limiting habit) Tolerance develops rapidly to physical and psychological effects No evidence of withdrawal
3,4-Methylenedioxy-N-methylamphetamine (MDMA)
Increased self-confidence, empathy, understanding, sensations of intimacy, communication, euphoria, and energy
Mydriasis Xerostomia Diaphoresis Nystagmus Bruxism Hyperpyrexia Rhabdomyolysis
Neurotoxic to brain serotonin system Leads to behavioral and physiological consequences Tolerance may develop in certain individuals Withdrawal: nausea, muscle stiffness, headache, loss of appetite, blurred vision, dry mouth, insomnia, depression, anxiety, fatigue, difficulty concentrating
Phencyclidine (PCP)
Aggression and anxiety Confusion, altered perceptions Dissociative experiences
Anesthetic effects Nystagmus
Flashbacks (up to 1 year following ingestion) Tolerance may develop in certain individuals No evidence of withdrawal
Ketamine
Slurred speech Amnesia Agitation Hallucinations
Respiratory depression and airway obstruction Muscular hypertonia Acute dystonia
Flashbacks (up to 1 year following ingestion) Tolerance may develop in certain individuals No evidence of withdrawal
